stem: A team repeatedly asks Claude Code to "read issue N from the tracker, reproduce it, and open a fix branch." They want to type /fix-issue 482 and have the issue number fill in automatically, and they want every teammate to get the command from the repository. What should they create?

options.text: A section in the project CLAUDE.md describing the fix-issue steps for Claude to follow.
options.why: CLAUDE.md is always-on guidance; it does not create a /fix-issue command or accept an argument.

options.text: A project skill or command file named fix-issue that uses $ARGUMENTS for the issue number.
options.why: Files in .claude/skills/ or .claude/commands/ become slash commands, and $ARGUMENTS is replaced with whatever follows the command.

options.text: A UserPromptSubmit hook that rewrites any prompt beginning with "fix-issue" into the full steps.
options.why: Hooks are for deterministic automation; rewriting prompts with a hook is a fragile substitute for the built-in command mechanism.

options.text: A personal skill in ~/.claude/skills/ that each developer copies from a shared wiki page.
options.why: Personal skills are not shared through the repository, so teammates would have to copy and update them by hand.

explanation: Custom slash commands are defined as project skills (.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md) or command files (.claude/commands/<name>.md), committed so the team shares them. Placeholders such as $ARGUMENTS insert the text typed after the command.

stem: A developer starts using Claude Code on a legacy service. The repository already has a short, hand-written CLAUDE.md that the team relies on. She wants Claude to add the build commands, test commands, and conventions it can discover, without losing the team's existing notes. What should she do?

options.text: Delete the existing CLAUDE.md, run /init to generate a fresh one, then paste the old notes back in.
options.why: Deleting the file is unnecessary and risks losing notes; /init already works with an existing CLAUDE.md.

options.text: Ask Claude to write the discovered commands into her own ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md file.
options.why: User-level instructions apply to all her projects and are not shared with the team, so the repository gains nothing.

options.text: Put the discovered commands in CLAUDE.local.md so the committed file stays untouched.
options.why: CLAUDE.local.md is personal and gitignored, so teammates would never see the build and test commands.

options.text: Run /init, review the improvements it suggests to the existing CLAUDE.md, and commit the result.
options.why: /init analyzes the codebase and, when a CLAUDE.md exists, suggests improvements instead of overwriting it.

explanation: /init bootstraps a project CLAUDE.md by analyzing the codebase for build commands, test instructions and conventions. With an existing file, it proposes improvements. The team should review the result and add guidance Claude cannot discover on its own.
reference: Claude Code docs — Memory (set up a project CLAUDE.md)

stem: A developer wraps claude -p in an internal web tool and wants users to see the answer appear token by token, then show cost and session details when the run ends. Which invocation fits best?

options.text: Use --output-format stream-json with --verbose and --include-partial-messages.
options.why: This streams newline-delimited JSON events, including partial text deltas, and ends with a result message carrying cost and session data.

options.text: Use --output-format json and display the result field once the process exits.
options.why: JSON output is a single object produced at the end of the run, so nothing appears until it finishes.

options.text: Use the default text output and forward each line of stdout to the browser the moment the process writes it.
options.why: Text output has no structured events and no cost or session metadata to show when the run ends.

options.text: Run an interactive session in a pseudo-terminal and scrape its screen output.
options.why: Scraping the interactive UI is brittle, and headless mode already provides structured streaming output.

explanation: Headless mode supports three output formats: text, json (one final object), and stream-json (newline-delimited events). Adding --include-partial-messages streams token-level deltas, and the final result message carries the response, cost and session metadata.
reference: Claude Code docs — Run Claude Code programmatically (stream responses)

stem: A developer runs a long refactor in auto mode and tells Claude early on, "Do not push to the remote." Hours later, after the conversation has been compacted, Claude pushes a branch. She wants to keep auto mode's low-prompt workflow but be certain pushes never happen without her. What should she do?

options.text: Switch to bypassPermissions so that behavior is predictable for the rest of the session.
options.why: bypassPermissions removes checks entirely, which makes an unwanted push more likely, not less.

options.text: Repeat "do not push" in the conversation every hour so a recent copy always survives compaction.
options.why: Conversational boundaries can still be lost when history is compacted; reminders reduce the risk but guarantee nothing.

options.text: Add a permissions deny rule for git push commands in her settings.
options.why: Deny rules are enforced in every permission mode, including auto, and do not depend on the conversation history.

options.text: Switch to acceptEdits mode so that shell commands such as git push prompt her first.
options.why: This would prompt before pushes, but it also brings back prompts for most shell commands, giving up the workflow she wants to keep.

explanation: Auto mode's safety checks treat boundaries stated in conversation as block signals, but those boundaries live in the transcript and can be lost to compaction. For a hard guarantee, use permission rules: deny rules apply in every mode.
reference: Claude Code docs — Permission modes (auto mode)

stem: A team shares a repository. They need (1) every developer's Claude Code sessions in this repo to use pnpm instead of npm, and (2) a custom code-reviewer subagent that builds up knowledge of this project's recurring issues over time and shares it with teammates through git. Which two configurations meet these needs? (Choose two.)

options.text: Rely on auto memory to learn "use pnpm" from each developer's corrections.
options.why: Auto memory is per-user and machine-local, so each developer would have to teach it separately, and nothing is shared.

options.text: Add "use pnpm, not npm" to the project CLAUDE.md and commit it.
options.why: The project CLAUDE.md loads for everyone working in the repository and is shared through version control.

options.text: Give the reviewer subagent user-scoped memory stored under ~/.claude.
options.why: User-scoped agent memory is personal and spans all projects, so it is neither project-specific nor shared through git.

options.text: Add "use pnpm, not npm" to each developer's ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md.
options.why: User-level files apply to every project on that machine and depend on each developer updating their own copy.

options.text: Give the reviewer subagent project-scoped memory stored under .claude/ and commit it.
options.why: Project-scoped agent memory is specific to this repository and can be shared through version control.

explanation: Put team-wide instructions in the project CLAUDE.md. Auto memory is for notes Claude takes for one user on one machine. Subagents can have persistent memory scoped to user, project, or local; project scope is the one that is repository-specific and shareable through git.
reference: Claude Code docs — Subagents (persistent memory); Memory

stem: A CI pipeline runs several jobs in parallel on the same runner and directory. Each job makes two calls: claude -p "review the diff" and then claude -p --continue "write the summary". Summaries sometimes describe another job's review. What is the most reliable fix?

options.text: Add --fork-session to the second call so that it gets its own session ID.
options.why: Forking still starts from whichever conversation --continue picked, which may belong to another job.

options.text: Combine review and summary into one prompt so each job makes only a single call.
options.why: This avoids the race but gives up the separate steps the pipeline was designed around, rather than fixing session selection.

options.text: Run the jobs in interactive mode so that each has its own terminal session.
options.why: Interactive sessions wait for terminal input and are not suited to unattended CI jobs.

options.text: Take session_id from the first call's JSON output and pass it to --resume.
options.why: Resuming by explicit session ID targets exactly the right conversation, whatever else is running in the directory.

explanation: --continue resumes the most recent conversation in the current directory, which is ambiguous when runs overlap. For scripted multi-step flows, capture session_id from --output-format json and resume that exact session with --resume.
reference: Claude Code docs — Run Claude Code programmatically; CLI reference

stem: A team wants Claude Code to hand security reviews to a dedicated reviewer that works in its own context, so the files it reads do not fill the main conversation. The reviewer must be limited to reading and searching code, Claude should use it automatically when a change needs a security review, and every teammate should get it from the repository. What should they create?

options.text: A subagent file in .claude/agents/ with a clear description and tools limited to Read, Grep and Glob.
options.why: Project subagents run in their own context window, the description tells Claude when to delegate, the tools field restricts access, and the file is shared through git.

options.text: A section in the project CLAUDE.md telling Claude to only read files when it is doing a security review.
options.why: CLAUDE.md is guidance in the main context; it neither isolates the review's context nor enforces a read-only tool set.

options.text: A subagent file in each developer's ~/.claude/agents/ directory with the same read-only tool list.
options.why: User-level subagents are personal and apply to all of that developer's projects; they are not shared through the repository.

options.text: A security-review prompt that developers paste when asking the built-in general-purpose subagent.
options.why: The general-purpose subagent has broad tool access, so the reviewer would not be limited to reading, and nothing makes Claude delegate automatically.

explanation: Custom subagents are Markdown files with frontmatter: description (when Claude should delegate), tools (an allowlist; omitted means inherit all), and optionally model and memory. Each runs in its own context window and returns a summary. Project subagents in .claude/agents/ are shared through version control; ~/.claude/agents/ holds personal ones.
